hops.title: Stonewashed jeans may never touch a stone
hops.text: The name promises stones, but your stonewashed jeans may never have met one. The traditional method tumbled each pair in a large washing machine with a kilogram or two of pumice. An enzyme called cellulase can do the job instead. It breaks tiny fiber ends off the surface of the cotton yarn, which loosens the dye, and the rubbing of the wash carries that dye away. In this wash the cotton is the substrate, and cellulase's active site fits the molecules cotton is made of.

sources.citation: Kuhad RC, Gupta R, Singh A. Microbial cellulases and their industrial applications. Enzyme Research 2011:280696 (2011).

hops.title: How a Yellowstone bacterium made PCR easier
hops.text: Scientists using an early version of PCR, a method for copying DNA, had a tedious chore. Every round needed high heat, the heat ruined their copying enzyme, and they had to add fresh enzyme again and again. Relief came from a bacterium living in Yellowstone's hot springs. Its copying enzyme, Taq, survived the heat, so the chore disappeared. That heat-proof enzyme later became a key ingredient in PCR-based tests for COVID-19. Both enzymes copied DNA, but only one could take the heat.

hops.title: Why Siamese cats have dark paws
hops.text: Why does a Siamese cat have a pale body but dark ears, paws, tail and face? In these cats, tyrosinase, the enzyme needed to make dark pigment, carries one changed building block, and the altered enzyme is thought to work only in cooler skin. About a century ago, researchers kept Siamese cats in the cold, and their pale fur darkened. Then they shaved a patch and warmed just that spot. The fur there grew back lighter. The cat's coat is a map of where one enzyme can work.

audio.title: A hot spring, a cat and a glass of milk
audio.transcript:
Okay, pull up a chair, because enzymes have been getting up to some very interesting things while nobody was looking. I have three stories for you: a hot spring, a cat, and a glass of milk.

Let's start with the hot spring. In nineteen sixty-four, a microbiologist named Thomas Brock stopped at Yellowstone to break up a long car trip and noticed the bright colors around a hot pool. Most of us would have admired the view and climbed back in the car. Not Brock. He kept coming back to take samples, and he found microbes living in water hotter than scientists of his day thought life could stand. A few years later, he and an undergraduate named Hudson Freeze described one of those bacteria and named it Thermus aquaticus. Yes, an undergraduate. It grows best at about seventy degrees Celsius, far hotter than your body.

Now here is where it gets good. Jump ahead to the nineteen eighties. Scientists had a new method called P C R, which makes huge numbers of copies of a piece of DNA. Wonderful method, one annoying problem. Every round of copying needed a hot step, and that heat ruined the enzyme doing the copying. So fresh enzyme had to be added, round after round after round, which was exactly as tedious as it sounds. Then they tried the copying enzyme from Brock's bacterium, an enzyme called Taq. Taq could take the heat, so nobody had to keep adding more. Decades later, when COVID nineteen arrived, many of the best tests for the virus used P C R, and that depends on a heat-proof enzyme like Taq. And it all traces back to a man who just wanted a break from driving.

Our second story has fur. You know the Siamese cat look: pale body, with dark ears, paws, tail and face. That pattern comes from an enzyme called tyrosinase, which the cat needs to make dark pigment. In Siamese cats, one building block of that enzyme is changed, and as far as scientists can tell, the enzyme stops working in warmer skin. So the warm middle of the cat stays pale, and the cooler tips turn dark. About a century ago, researchers put this to the test, and honestly, the cats must have had questions. They kept Siamese cats in the cold, and the pale fur darkened. Then they shaved a patch and kept just that spot warm. When the hair grew back, it came in lighter than the fur around it. Same cat, same genes, different temperature, different color.

Our last story may be about you, or someone you eat lunch with. Milk contains a sugar called lactose, and the enzyme that splits it is lactase, which works in your small intestine. Around the world, about two out of three adults digest lactose poorly, mostly because their bodies make less lactase after infancy. So if milk does not sit well with you, you have plenty of company. Without enough lactase, some of the lactose travels on to the colon, where bacteria break it down and make gas and fluid, and that can bring on an upset stomach. But here is the part I love: the amount matters. Many people with lactose intolerance can have about a cup of milk with mild symptoms or none at all, though it varies from person to person. That is your enzyme lesson, right there in the kitchen. A limited amount of enzyme can only handle so much substrate.

One enzyme that shrugs off heat, one that colors a cat by temperature, and one whose supply decides how a glass of milk goes down.
